lead: A beam's bending stiffness depends less on how much material the cross-section has than on how far that material sits from the neutral axis; the second moment of area measures that spread. Take every small piece of the cross-section, multiply its area by the square of its distance from the axis, and add. The result, written I, carries units of mm⁴. It appears wherever bending or deflection is calculated: steel joists, timber beams, a bus chassis, an aircraft wing spar.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the element of area and its distance from an axis, and basic integration for the rectangle derivation.

blocks.text: Take a flat area: a beam cross-section, a plate, a hatch cover. Fix an axis in its plane. Cut the area into tiny pieces of area dA, and let y be the perpendicular distance from the axis to a piece. The second moment of area about that axis is the sum of y² dA over all the pieces.

blocks.where: Iₓ is the second moment of area about the x-axis, in mm⁴; dA is the area of an element, in mm²; y is the perpendicular distance of that element from the x-axis, in mm; the integral covers the whole area.

blocks.text: Units come out as mm² × mm² = mm⁴, length to the fourth power. Every answer must carry mm⁴ or m⁴; a bare number is incomplete.

The name needs care. Many books call this the “moment of inertia of an area”. No mass is involved and nothing turns; the quantity is pure geometry, area weighted by squared distance. The name survives because the algebra is identical to the mass moment of inertia, where mass replaces area (see 4.8). Some syllabi say “second moment of area” for exactly this reason. Both names mean the same integral.

Why the square? When a beam bends, a fibre at distance y from the neutral axis stretches in proportion to y and carries stress in proportion to that stretch; the moment it resists is its force times y again. Two factors of y. Material far from the axis therefore does far more work than material near it, which is why steel joists are I-shaped rather than square.

sections.h3: Rectangle by a strip, centroidal and base

blocks.text: Take a rectangle of width b and depth h. The centroidal axis is parallel to the base and passes through the centre, so the strip at height y from that axis runs from y = −h/2 to y = +h/2.

items: Choose the axis. Here it is the horizontal centroidal axis.
Take a strip parallel to the axis at distance y, of thickness dy. Its area is dA = b dy.
Write the integrand: y² dA = b y² dy.
Integrate between the limits: I = ∫ b y² dy = b[y³/3] from −h/2 to h/2.
Put in the limits: (b/3)(h³/8 + h³/8) = b h³/12.

blocks.text: For the base as axis the strip runs from y = 0 to y = h, and the same steps give I = b h³/3, four times larger. The parallel axis theorem of 4.5 checks this: the area b h sits at distance h/2 from the base, so b h³/12 + b h (h/2)² = b h³/12 + b h³/4 = b h³/3.

Two warnings. The formula b h³/12 belongs to the centroidal axis only; about any other axis, integrate again or use the parallel axis theorem. And h is always the dimension perpendicular to the axis you are taking, not a fixed label for the longer side.

sections.h3: Standard shapes, and why depth beats width

head: Shape
Axis
I (mm⁴)
rows: Hollow circle, D outside, d inside

blocks.text: Read the third column as the formula to quote. The triangle's centroidal axis is h/3 above the base, and the 36 in the denominator comes from that offset. For a circle every diameter passes through the centroid and gives the same value, so any diameter may be named; for other shapes the axis must always be stated. A hollow circle uses the outer D and the inner d in the same bracket, subtracted, because the hole takes away the material nearest the axis.

Scaling. Take a plank 100 mm wide. At 100 mm depth, I = 100 × 100³/12 = 8.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴. At 200 mm depth, I = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Twice the area, eight times the stiffness. Doubling the width would give only twice. The extra material in a deep beam sits near the outer fibres, where y² is large; extra material added sideways sits near the axis, where it earns little.

That is the design argument for the I-section, the box girder and the hollow tube: keep the material away from the neutral axis. It is also why turning a plank on its edge changes a springy board into a stiff beam. A beam's stiffness in bending comes from I, not from A; two sections of equal area can differ severalfold.

examples.question: A timber beam has a rectangular cross-section 120 mm wide and 200 mm deep. (a) Find the second moment of area about the centroidal axis parallel to the base. (b) Find it about the base itself. (c) The beam is turned on its side so that the depth becomes 120 mm; find the new centroidal value and the ratio of the two.
steps: Identify b and h. For an axis parallel to the base, the depth is the dimension perpendicular to that axis: b = 120 mm, h = 200 mm.
Check (b) by the parallel axis theorem: 80 × 10⁶ + (120 × 200)(100)² = 80 × 10⁶ + 240 × 10⁶ = 320 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Agrees.
(c) On its side the depth is 120 mm and the width is 200 mm: 120³ = 1,728,000 mm³, so I = 200 × 1,728,000 / 12 = 28,800,000 mm⁴ = 28.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
Ratio of the two centroidal values: 80 / 28.8 = 2.78. Laid on its side the beam is 2.78 times easier to bend, with no change in the amount of timber.
examples.answer: I = 80 × 10⁶ mm⁴ about the centroidal axis, 320 × 10⁶ mm⁴ about the base, and 28.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴ on its side, so the beam used on edge is 2.78 times stiffer.
examples.check:
b = 120.0
h = 200.0
Ic = b * h**3 / 12
Ib = b * h**3 / 3
Is = h * b**3 / 12
ratio = Ic / Is
print(Ic)
print(Ib)
print(Is)
print(round(ratio, 2))

traps: b h³/12 is for the centroidal axis. If the question says “about the base”, it is b h³/3. Read the axis before writing the formula.
Circle formulas: π d⁴/64 takes the diameter d, while π r⁴/4 takes the radius r. Feeding a diameter into the radius form makes the answer 16 times too large.
Units: I is length to the fourth power, and 1 m⁴ = 10¹² mm⁴. Converting one line to metres and leaving the next in millimetres costs marks silently.
b and h are not fixed labels for the two sides. h is always the dimension perpendicular to the axis you are taking, and examiners rotate sections deliberately.
Do not confuse mm⁴ with kg m². If the question gives a density or asks about rotation, it wants the mass moment of inertia of 4.8, not this one.

quiz.q: Define the second moment of area of a plane area about the x-axis and state its units.
quiz.a: Iₓ = ∫ y² dA, where y is the perpendicular distance of the element dA from the x-axis. Units are mm⁴, that is, length to the fourth power.

quiz.q: Why is the name “moment of inertia of an area” misleading?
quiz.a: No mass and no rotation are involved. The quantity is a purely geometric sum of area times squared distance. It shares its algebra, not its physics, with the mass moment of inertia.

quiz.q: A rectangle is doubled in depth, its width unchanged. What happens to I about the centroidal axis, and why?
quiz.a: I becomes 2³ = 8 times larger, because I = b h³/12 and h enters cubed. The area has only doubled, so each unit of area is doing more work.

quiz.q: A rectangle is 60 mm wide and 100 mm deep. Find I about the centroidal axis parallel to the 60 mm side.
quiz.a: h = 100 mm is perpendicular to that axis. I = b h³/12 = 60 × 1,000,000 / 12 = 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

quiz.q: Find the second moment of area of a solid circular shaft of diameter 40 mm about a diameter.
Two beams use about the same amount of material: 100 mm × 200 mm (20,000 mm²) and 150 mm × 150 mm (22,500 mm²). Which resists bending better about the horizontal centroidal axis, and by how much?
quiz.a: I₁ = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴; I₂ = 150 × 150³/12 = 42.19 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The 100 × 200 beam has 1.58 times the second moment of area even though it has slightly less area, because its material lies further from the axis.

quiz.q: A hollow tube has outside diameter 100 mm and inside diameter 80 mm. Compare its I about a diameter with that of a solid 100 mm shaft, and comment.
quiz.a: Tube: I = π(100⁴ − 80⁴)/64 = π(10⁸ − 4.096 × 10⁷)/64 = 2.898 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Solid: π × 10⁸/64 = 4.909 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The bore removes 64% of the area but only 41% of I, because the material it removes is the material closest to the axis.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design codes work with the section modulus Z = I / y_max rather than I alone, and with a plastic modulus once a beam may yield; search “section modulus”. Finite element programs never integrate strips by hand — they sum over element Gauss points — but the definition stays exactly the one in this chapter. Read the unit and sign conventions of I in a national code before your first design project.
